classification.difficultyReason: Direct percentage-to-decimal conversions, including mixed and fractional percentages.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses percentage-to-decimal conversion. Parts g and h also require converting a fractional percentage to a decimal percentage. None of the supplied reuse candidates has the same original task.
questions.methodNote: The first review bullet instructs students to move the decimal point two places to the left when converting a percentage to a decimal, illustrated by 27% = 0.27. Fractional percentages are first written as decimal percentages.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct percentage-to-decimal conversions, including mixed and fractional percentages.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert percentages, including fractional percentages, to fractions and simplify.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess this conversion and reduction to lowest terms. The supplied reuse candidates have different complete tasks and are unsuitable.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 teaches conversion of a percentage to a fraction by multiplying by 1/100, including a fractional percentage, then simplifying.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert percentages, including fractional percentages, to fractions and simplify.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct conversions of fractions, mixed numerals and decimals to percentages, including values greater than one.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses conversion to percentage form. All supplied reuse candidates have different complete source tasks, so none is reused.
questions.methodNote: The inspected review states that a decimal or fraction is converted to a percentage by multiplying by 100%, demonstrated with 0.35 and 3/5. Mixed numerals are represented as improper fractions before multiplication; recurring results remain exact.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct conversions of fractions, mixed numerals and decimals to percentages, including values greater than one.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert between percentage, fraction and decimal forms and simplify fractions.

questions.mappingNote: All six rows assess equivalent percentage, fraction and decimal representations. The supplied reuse candidates contain different complete tasks.
questions.methodNote: Convert percentages to decimals by dividing by 100 and to fractions by multiplying by 1/100, then simplify. Convert decimals or fractions to percentages by multiplying by 100%.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert between percentage, fraction and decimal forms and simplify fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly convert each percentage to a decimal and multiply, rounding to two decimal places.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess finding a percentage of a quantity. None of the supplied reuse candidates matches this complete task.
questions.methodNote: The percentage-of-a-quantity demonstration converts the percentage to a decimal or fraction, then multiplies the quantity by it. Decimal multiplication is used here, retaining exact products before rounding.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly convert each percentage to a decimal and multiply, rounding to two decimal places.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct percentage calculations involving money, including decimal and fractional percentages.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess finding a percentage of a monetary quantity. Parts e and f require converting fractional percentages before multiplication. None of the supplied reuse candidates has the same original task.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 teaches converting a percentage to a decimal or fraction and multiplying the quantity by it. The worked solutions use decimal conversion and retain currency units.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct percentage calculations involving money, including decimal and fractional percentages.

classification.difficultyReason: Express each first quantity as a percentage of the second in matching units, rounding to one decimal place.

questions.mappingNote: All four pairs already have matching units. The directly assessed skill is expressing one quantity as a percentage of another, followed by rounding to one decimal place.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 instructs students to express both quantities in the same unit, form the first quantity divided by the second, and multiply by 100%. Its 32 cm and 2.4 m demonstration models the ratio method. Pages 3 and 11 were inspected; their reverse-percentage and percentage-change methods are unnecessary here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express each first quantity as a percentage of the second in matching units, rounding to one decimal place.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert to common units, including weeks through days to hours, then form the directed ratio and convert to a percentage; the unit-conversion step is explicitly prompted.

questions.mappingNote: Every part assesses one quantity as a percentage of another after a unit conversion. Length conversion is supported by page 2; original teaching evidence for currency and calendar/time conversions remains missing.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 instructs students to convert quantities to the same unit, form the first quantity divided by the second, and multiply by 100%. Its example converts metres to centimetres. Pages 3 and 11 were inspected but do not supply the currency or calendar/time conversion prerequisites.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert quantities to matching units, calculate their ratio as a percentage, and round to two decimal places.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate a percentage of a given population and round to a whole number of students.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed operation is finding 7% of 640. Whole-student rounding is consistent with the population-count example on page 11 and the answer key.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 teaches finding a percentage of a quantity by converting the percentage to a decimal or fraction and multiplying. Page 11 demonstrates rounding a calculated population count to the nearest integer. Page 3 was inspected; its reverse-percentage and commission methods are not required here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a percentage of a given population and round to a whole number of students.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert each given percentage to a decimal and multiply by the sample mass.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess finding a percentage of the given 2.6 g sample. Neither requires percentage change or recovering an original amount.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 teaches converting a percentage to a decimal and multiplying the quantity by it. Page 3 Example 2(a) demonstrates the percentage, decimal substitution and result on successive lines. Page 11 was inspected but its percentage-change method is unnecessary here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert each given percentage to a decimal and multiply by the sample mass.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate 65% of the match duration, then interpret the decimal fraction of a minute and convert it to seconds.

questions.mappingNote: The principal calculation finds 65% of 94 minutes. Expressing the result in the requested units additionally assesses decimal-minute conversion.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 teaches converting a percentage to a decimal and multiplying the quantity by it. Pages 3 and 11 also demonstrate decimal percentage factors. None of these pages teaches converting fractional minutes to seconds.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a percentage of a duration, then convert the fractional minute to seconds.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish the 110% increase from the final membership; the two parts scaffold calculating new members before adding the original membership.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses 110% of the original membership to find the increase. Part b adds that increase to the original membership. Percentage increase and decrease is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 teaches finding a percentage of a quantity by converting the percentage to a decimal and multiplying. Page 3 illustrates percentage multiplication in financial contexts. Page 11 explains that a percentage increase is measured against the original amount and explicitly recognises calculating the increase separately and adding it on.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate an increase of 110% of the original membership and then the resulting total.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught reversal by dividing each known portion by its decimal percentage; the smaller percentage and fractional result add no new method.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts recover the whole from a known percentage of it. Reverse percentage problems is the closest catalogue skill, although these parts involve a percentage portion rather than a changed final amount.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 instructs division by the known percentage to find the original amount. Page 3 Example 1 replaces the percentage by its decimal and divides the known amount; Example 2(b) repeats this reversal. Page 11 concerns percentage change and is not needed for this task.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover each original quantity by dividing a given percentage amount by its decimal percentage.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the deposit as the given percentage portion of the full price and divide by 0.30 using the taught reversal.

questions.mappingNote: The deposit is a known percentage of the full price. Dividing 570 by 0.30 follows Example 1 directly; reverse-percentage-problems is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces finding an original amount by dividing the known portion by its percentage. Example 1 on pages 2–3 reverses multiplication by the percentage, replaces the percentage with its decimal equivalent and divides.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover the full price by dividing a given deposit by its percentage expressed as a decimal.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover selling price by dividing commission by the decimal commission rate, then round where requested.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly apply the commission reversal demonstrated in Example 2(b); financial-percentage-problems is the closest supplied financial-context skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 2(b) writes commission as selling price multiplied by the percentage, then reverses the calculation by dividing commission by the decimal rate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reverse a commission calculation by dividing the commission by its decimal rate.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine whether sales imply profit or loss, calculate the difference, and express it as a percentage of costs rather than sales.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess Example 3's percentage profit or loss on costs. Part a produces an exact percentage; part b requires rounding.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 calculates profit as sales minus costs or loss as costs minus sales, then divides by total costs and multiplies by 100%.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate profit or loss, then express it as a percentage of the given costs.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse the profit or loss percentage to recover costs, then choose addition for profit and subtraction for loss to obtain sales.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly applies Example 4 to 5.4% profit; part b applies the same reverse-percentage calculation to a 6.5% loss and subtracts the loss to obtain sales.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 on page 5 writes profit as costs multiplied by the percentage, reverses using division, and adds profit to costs for total sales. Page 4 establishes loss as costs minus sales, giving sales as costs minus loss.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover costs from a percentage profit or loss, then calculate total sales.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest parts identify the applicable marginal band from total tax, remove tax from lower bands, reverse the remaining rate, and restore the income threshold.

questions.mappingNote: The question repeats Example 5's fictional Plusionta tax rules exactly. Part a applies the demonstrated band calculations; part b expresses those results as percentages of the corresponding incomes; part c reverses the same calculations.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 calculates tax separately on each successive income band and adds the band amounts. Reverse calculations subtract tax accumulated in lower bands, divide the remaining tax by the marginal rate and restore the band threshold.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate progressive tax across bands, express tax as a percentage of income and reverse the appropriate marginal calculation.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate annual interest and substitute known values into the supplied simple-interest formula.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the annual-interest rule directly; part b explicitly requests the formula demonstrated in Example 6.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 defines annual simple interest as P × R and total interest as I = PRT, with a decimal annual rate and time in years. Example 6 on page 7 demonstrates substitution, percentage-to-decimal conversion and evaluation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate annual interest and substitute known values into the supplied simple-interest formula.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of principal, annual rate and time into the simple-interest formula.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess total simple interest from a given principal, annual percentage rate and investment duration.
questions.methodNote: Use I = PRT, convert the annual percentage rate to a decimal, and substitute the time in years, following Example 6.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of principal, annual rate and time into the simple-interest formula.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute supplied interest, principal and time into the taught simple-interest relationship, divide to isolate the rate, and express it as a percentage.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess the reverse use of the simple interest formula demonstrated in Example 7; interest is already supplied, so no repayment subtraction is required.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 substitutes the known interest, principal and time into I = PRT, solves for R and expresses the annual rate as a percentage.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute three known quantities into the simple interest formula and solve for the annual percentage rate.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the interest, principal and annual rate into the simple-interest formula and solve for time.

questions.mappingNote: Page 6 defines simple interest and its formula. Page 7 teaches reverse use of the formula to find an unknown pronumeral, directly supporting both time calculations.
questions.methodNote: Use I = PRT with the annual rate expressed as a decimal; substitute the three known quantities and solve for T in years.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute the interest, principal and annual rate into the simple-interest formula and solve for time.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the interest, annual rate and time into the simple-interest formula and solve for the principal.

questions.mappingNote: Page 6 defines principal and the simple-interest formula. Page 7 explicitly teaches reverse use of the formula to find any unknown from the other three quantities; Question 23 applies this method to P.
questions.methodNote: Use I = PRT with the annual percentage rate expressed as a decimal and time in years. Substitute the three known quantities and solve the resulting equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute the interest, annual rate and time into the simple-interest formula and solve for the principal.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply a single increase multiplier to each supplied monetary amount.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly apply the one-step increase method demonstrated on page 11.
questions.methodNote: Identify the new amount as (100 + percentage increase)% of the original, then multiply by the corresponding decimal multiplier.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply a single increase multiplier to each supplied monetary amount.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply a single decrease multiplier to each supplied monetary amount.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly apply the one-step decrease method demonstrated on page 11.
questions.methodNote: Identify the remaining amount as (100 − percentage decrease)% of the original, then multiply by the corresponding decimal multiplier.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply a single decrease multiplier to each supplied monetary amount.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied increase multiplier in context and round a vehicle estimate when necessary.

questions.mappingNote: The question supplies the multiplier explicitly. Page 11 demonstrates the same multiplier method and rounding a count to the nearest integer.
questions.methodNote: A 12% increase gives 112% of the original quantity, so multiply by 1.12; round counts to whole objects.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the supplied increase multiplier in context and round a vehicle estimate when necessary.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied decrease multiplier and round measurements to the nearest millimetre.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded method cue directly matches the remaining-percentage calculation on page 11.
questions.methodNote: A 38% decrease leaves 62% of the original measurement; multiply by 0.62 and round as requested.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the supplied decrease multiplier and round measurements to the nearest millimetre.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the earlier number as the percentage base, calculate relative change, and identify whether each result represents an increase or decrease.

questions.mappingNote: Example 8 on page 12 explicitly teaches new divided by old, multiplied by 100%, followed by comparison with 100%. Values above 100% indicate increases and values below 100% indicate decreases.
questions.methodNote: Express the new quantity as a percentage of the original, then find its difference from 100%; retain exact values until final rounding.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare final and original counts as percentages, distinguish increases from decreases and round the change.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate each increase or decrease into the percentage remaining and divide the new amount by the corresponding multiplier.

questions.mappingNote: Part a divides by 0.90 after a 10% decrease; part b divides by 1.10 after a 10% increase. Both directly assess finding the original amount using the taught reversal method.
questions.methodNote: Identify the percentage of the original represented by the new amount, convert it to a multiplier, then reverse multiplication by dividing. Page 12 Example 9 demonstrates reversal after a decrease; page 13 demonstrates both directions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the multiplier for a single percentage change and divide to recover the original amount.

classification.difficultyReason: The task supplies both the 1.14 multiplier and the instruction to divide, leaving substitution and whole-share rounding.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses the original shareholding after a percentage increase. The source supplies the multiplier and division instruction, so reverse-percentage-problems is the closest primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Identify the new holding as 114% of the original and reverse multiplication by 1.14 through division. Pages 12–13 demonstrate division by the percentage multiplier to recover an original amount.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly supplied reverse-percentage multiplier to three current shareholdings.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret each theory as an increase or decrease multiplier, divide the present volume to recover the original, and round to tens.

questions.mappingNote: Page 11 introduces percentage multipliers; page 12 reverses increases and decreases; page 13 Example 10 explicitly demonstrates both reverse calculations. Question 8 carries the printed Example 10 reference and assesses this method for four lake-volume theories.
questions.methodNote: Identify the present amount as (100 plus or minus the percentage change)% of the original amount, then divide by the corresponding decimal multiplier. Round only the final original volume.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reverse four percentage changes, including an increase exceeding 100%, and round original volumes to the nearest 10 megalitres.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert the 35% discount into 65% payable and multiply each marked price by 0.65.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts ask for a discounted price from a marked price. The directly assessed method is multiplication by 1−0.35=0.65; reverse-percentage methods are unnecessary.
questions.methodNote: Identify the percentage remaining after the decrease and multiply the original amount by its decimal multiplier. Example 11(a) applies this directly to discounted prices.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the same percentage-decrease multiplier to four marked prices.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the discounted amount as 45% of the original and reverse the taught multiplier by division, rounding to cents.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts recover an original price after a 55% discount, so the directly assessed skill is reverse percentage problems. The multiplier is 0.45; direct percentage calculation alone does not complete the task.
questions.methodNote: Identify the percentage remaining after the decrease, then reverse multiplication by dividing the discounted price by the remaining decimal multiplier. Page 13 Example 11 explicitly applies this method to discounts and rounds original prices to the nearest cent.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the remaining percentage after a discount and divide by its multiplier to recover each original price.

classification.difficultyReason: Select between forward percentage change, reversing a multiplier and finding a signed percentage change across nine table rows.

questions.mappingNote: Rows a–c use forward multipliers; rows d–f reverse those multipliers, including the share-price context of Example 10; rows g–i apply Example 8's ratio method and retain negative decreases.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 teaches multiplying by 1 plus or minus the decimal rate. Page 12 finds percentage change using new divided by old, expressed as a percentage, then subtracting 100%. Pages 12–13 reverse percentage changes by dividing by the corresponding multiplier.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select between forward percentage change, reversing a multiplier and finding a signed percentage change across nine table rows.

classification.difficultyReason: Part c requires distinguishing GST from the inclusive price, recovering the pre-tax whole from its 10% portion, and then adding the tax.

questions.mappingNote: All nine items assess GST; part c first reverses the tax component, then adds GST.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 identifies the inclusive price as 110% of the pre-tax price, multiplies by 1.10 and reverses by dividing by 1.10. GST itself is 10% of the pre-tax price.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses GST to find inclusive prices, reverse inclusive prices and recover prices from the tax component.

classification.difficultyReason: Form the inflation multiplier 1.034 and choose multiplication for current prices or division for previous prices.

questions.mappingNote: The six items apply the 1.034 multiplier in forward and reverse directions; reverse percentage problems is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 13 estimates current prices by multiplying by the inflation multiplier and previous prices by dividing by it.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Applies and reverses a single inflation multiplier.

classification.difficultyReason: Finds restoration percentages using the changed amount as the new percentage base.

questions.mappingNote: Each restoration asks for a percentage change relative to the changed value, rather than simply negating the original percentage.
questions.methodNote: Apply the initial percentage multiplier, express the desired value as a percentage of the current value, then compare with 100%, following Example 8 and the reversal discussion.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Finds restoration percentages using the changed amount as the new percentage base.

classification.difficultyReason: Determines inverse percentage changes without supplied original quantities.

questions.mappingNote: All eight items assess restoration percentages; the changed quantity is the denominator when expressing the restoration as a percentage.
questions.methodNote: Use percentage multipliers and Example 8's ratio of desired to current amount, followed by comparison with 100%. Choosing an original quantity of 100 makes the percentage base explicit.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determines inverse percentage changes without supplied original quantities.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply successive increase or decrease multipliers, using a power for ten identical increases as taught.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses increase multipliers 1.05, 1.08 and 1.10; part b uses decrease multipliers 0.92, 0.93 and 0.94; part c uses the tenth power of 1.10. All directly assess repeated percentage change.
questions.methodNote: Examples 14–16 and the page 20 summary apply successive increase or decrease multipliers. Page 21 introduces powers for equal successive changes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of successive percentage multipliers, including a power for ten equal increases.

classification.difficultyReason: The complete product of percentage multipliers is supplied, so the task requires multiplication by the starting price and rounding.

questions.mappingNote: The question explicitly supplies three successive increase factors; applying their product directly assesses repeated percentage change.
questions.methodNote: Example 14 multiplies the original amount successively by the increase factors, retaining calculator precision until the final rounding.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the three supplied percentage multipliers to the original price.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate four successive increases into multipliers, including increases above 100%, and apply their product to each original dividend.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess successive percentage increases. The teacher answers identify the intended result as the final dividend rather than the sum of four annual dividends.
questions.methodNote: Example 14 multiplies the original quantity successively by each percentage-increase multiplier, retaining exact calculator values until final rounding. Here D denotes the dividend after the fourth increase; currency answers are rounded to the nearest cent.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert four successive increases, including increases greater than 100%, into multipliers.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine seven annual percentage increases, interpret the overall increase and apply the multiplier to three starting amounts.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 repeats the same 1.06 multiplier seven times and assesses both the combined percentage increase and resulting amounts, so repeated percentage change is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 14 applies successive increase multipliers to the original amount, keeps unrounded values for later calculations and subtracts 100% from the final percentage of the original to obtain the overall increase.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine seven annual percentage increases, interpret the overall increase and apply the multiplier to three starting amounts.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine four different decrease multipliers and interpret the resulting multiplier as an overall percentage decrease.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 applies precisely this repeated-decrease method to four successive years; repeated-percentage-change is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 18 introduces successive multiplication of percentage-change factors. Example 15 on page 19 converts decreases into remaining-percentage multipliers, multiplies them and interprets the remaining proportion to find the overall loss.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine four different decrease multipliers and interpret the resulting multiplier as an overall percentage decrease.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the increase and decrease multiplicatively, then interpret the product relative to 1 as the overall percentage change.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess repeated percentage changes with one increase followed by one decrease; the combined multiplier determines the overall decrease.
questions.methodNote: Example 16 multiplies successive increase and decrease factors, converts the combined multiplier to a percentage of the original, and subtracts 100% to identify the overall change. Its following note explains why adding the original percentage changes is inappropriate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine two percentage multipliers and interpret the resulting overall decrease.

classification.difficultyReason: The reverse chronological divisions and all multipliers are supplied; retain precision while extracting the requested intermediate prices.

questions.mappingNote: The task reverses several percentage changes and recovers intermediate and original prices; repeated percentage change is primary, with reverse percentage problems secondary.
questions.methodNote: Example 17 reverses successive changes by dividing the final quantity by the percentage multipliers. Page 21 states the corresponding reverse-multiplier rule. Apply the question's specified successive divisions in reverse chronological order without intermediate rounding.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reverse three successive percentage increases, retaining unrounded intermediate values.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply an equal annual decrease five times and interpret the combined multiplier as a percentage decrease.

questions.mappingNote: All three monetary responses apply the annual multiplier 0.82 five times; part b interprets the combined multiplier. Repeated percentage change is the most directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 15 multiplies by the remaining proportion after each decrease. Example 18 replaces successive equal multipliers by a power and interprets the remaining proportion to find the total percentage decrease.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply an equal annual decrease five times and interpret the combined multiplier as a percentage decrease.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse four equal percentage increases by dividing by the combined multiplier.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts reverse four hourly increases of 18%, using current population divided by 1.18 to the fourth power. Repeated percentage change is the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 17 reverses successive percentage changes by division. Example 18 and the reversing summary combine equal multipliers using powers and round population answers to the nearest integer.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reverse four equal percentage increases by dividing by the combined multiplier.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply a repeated decrease using powers, then reverse the multiplier to recover earlier temperatures.

questions.mappingNote: Every response applies or reverses the same 16% decrease across multiple minutes; repeated percentage change is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 15 converts percentage decreases to remaining-value multipliers. Example 17 reverses successive changes by division. Page 21 and Example 18 express repeated equal multipliers using powers and reverse them by division.

questions.mappingNote: The principal plus P/10 interest gives a final amount of 11P/10. Cancelling P leaves a two-period growth factor of 1.1. Recovering its annual factor requires a positive square root; original teaching evidence for that prerequisite was not supplied.
